core.text: The everyday way to tell someone *not* to do something is **noli / nolite + infinitive (the polite 'don't …')**. *Nōlī* is the command form of *nōlō* (I do not want), so *Nōlī timēre!* is literally 'don't want to fear' — 'don't be afraid'. To several people say *nōlīte*. The verb after it is the plain infinitive (the 'to' form), so a deponent verb (passive-looking endings, active meaning: loquitur = he speaks) keeps its -ī / -ārī / -ērī infinitive: *Nōlī imitārī!* Latin name: *prohibitiō: nōlī cum īnfīnītīvō*.
English makes a negative command with *don't* plus the verb: *don't go*. Latin does the same job with a helping verb, 'be unwilling to go'.
nōlī (to one person) or nōlīte (to several) + infinitive = 'do not …'.

*Nōlī* is itself **the imperative (the command form)** of *nōlō*; the real action is the infinitive that follows. So *Nōlī abīre!* pairs with the positive *Abī!* (go away!), not with *nōn abī*, which Latin never says.

more.text: The learner's notes (week 20) call this a 'polite prohibition' and note that *nē* + imperative (*nē timē*) exists but is rare, mostly in poetry. Prose also uses *nē* with **the perfect subjunctive (the 'have done' form: nescio quid fecerit; ne timueris = don't be afraid)**: *nē timuerīs!* — the same meaning, a shade more urgent (chapter XXXII).
Other polite refusals use *cavē* (beware) + subjunctive: *cavē cadās* — mind you don't fall.
This is the ordinary, courteous way to forbid something, and it is what you will meet almost every time.
It is the *nōlī* in front that makes it a prohibition, not the ending behind: after *nōlī* the verb is always the infinitive, whatever shape that infinitive has — *rīdēre*, *esse*, *īre*, *loquī*.

teach.title: What it does

notice.ask: Which word in each sentence tells somebody not to do something?

teach.say: To tell somebody *not* to do something, Latin does not put a 'not' in front of the command. It uses nōlī / nōlīte + infinitive (the polite 'don't …'): *nōlī clāmāre* is literally 'be unwilling to shout', which is simply 'don't shout'.

check.ask: Tap the word that turns this order into a 'don't'.

teach.title: nōlī to one person, nōlīte to more than one
teach.say: *Nōlī* and *nōlīte* are the imperative (the command form) of *nōlō* 'not to want'. Say *nōlī* to one person — *nōlī dormīre, Mārce* — and *nōlīte* to two or more — *nōlīte dormīre, puerī*. Nothing else in the sentence changes; that first word alone says how many people are being told.

show.say: nōlī to one, nōlīte to several

check.ask: Fill the blank with the form used when more than one person is being told.

teach.title: The verb that follows is the infinitive
teach.say: Whatever you are forbidding goes into the infinitive (the 'to' form), never into a command form: *nōlīte dūcere*, not *nōlīte dūcite*. So the pattern is always two verbs — *nōlī* or *nōlīte* first, its infinitive last — with whatever else the sentence needs sitting between them: *nōlī epistulam meam legere*.

check.ask: legere — which form of the verb is it, and why not lege?

teach.title: Any verb at all, even the odd ones
teach.say: Whichever infinitive a verb happens to have is the one you use. A deponent verb (passive-looking endings, active meaning: loquitur = he speaks) has an infinitive in *-ī*: *nōlī loquī*. *Sum* has *esse*: *nōlīte improbī esse*. *Eō* has *īre*: *nōlīte īre*. The construction never changes; only that second word does.

check.ask: Tap the infinitive that this prohibition forbids.

teach.title: Telling it from the plain command
teach.say: A plain command tells somebody to do something: *tacē!*, be quiet. Put *nōlī* in front and the verb behind it forbids instead, and is always the infinitive: *nōlī rīdēre!*, don't laugh. A command form standing alone, with no *nōlī* in front of it, is an order.

check.ask: Tap the word that forbids, not the one that orders.

teach.title: Using it
teach.say: Latin will happily wedge the person's name between the two halves — *nōlī, Quīnte, ex lectulō surgere* — and the pattern still holds: find *nōlī* or *nōlīte*, then look to the end of the sentence for its infinitive. Now build the second half yourself: the forbidden verb never comes out as a command.

check.ask: Nōlī iterum in aquam ____ ! Write the form of cadō that has to follow nōlī.
